clinicalPearls: OSA diagnosis requires either symptoms of nocturnal breathing disturbance (snoring, snorting, gasping, breathing pauses) impairing quality of life or unexplained daytime sleepiness/fatigue, PLUS at least 5 obstructive apnoeas/hypopnoeas per hour of sleep (apnoea-hypopnoea index, AHI) on a sleep study; OSA may also be diagnosed without symptoms if AHI is at least 15 episodes/h (p.2277-2278).
Each apnoea/hypopnoea is a reduction in breathing for at least 10 s, commonly causing a fall in oxygen saturation of at least 3% or a cortical arousal (p.2278).
The major risk factors for OSA are obesity, male sex, and older age; roughly 40-60% of cases are attributable to excess weight, but the absence of obesity does NOT exclude the diagnosis (p.2278).

Snoring is the most common symptom, but its absence does NOT exclude OSA because pharyngeal collapse can occur without tissue vibration; the most common daytime symptom is excessive sleepiness, though women preferentially report fatigue rather than sleepiness (p.2279).
Dyspnoea is unusual in OSA, and its absence generally distinguishes OSA from paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, nocturnal asthma, and acid reflux with laryngospasm (p.2279).

Overnight in-laboratory polysomnography (PSG) is the gold standard for diagnosis; a negative in-lab PSG usually rules out OSA, but false-negatives can occur with night-to-night variation, insufficient REM sleep, or less supine sleep than typical (p.2279).
Home sleep tests recording only respiratory and cardiac channels are a cost-effective option; when prior probability of OSA is high, a negative home study should be followed by PSG (p.2279).

CPAP is the standard medical therapy with the highest level of evidence; it acts as a mechanical splint to hold the airway open during sleep, and auto-titrating (APAP) home devices have eliminated the need for titration studies in many patients (p.2281).

Although CPAP reduces 24-h ambulatory blood pressure, the overall effect is modest (averaging 2-4 mmHg), with larger improvements in patients with high AHI, daytime sleepiness, or resistant hypertension (p.2280-2281).

Large randomized trials have FAILED to show that CPAP reduces cardiovascular/stroke events or prolongs survival, possibly because sleepy patients (who may have the greatest risk) were excluded and because of limited treatment adherence (p.2281).

Central sleep apnoea (CSA) is less common than OSA and may occur alone or, more often, combined with obstructive events as mixed apnoeas; it is often driven by increased sensitivity to PCO2 causing unstable breathing, and a prolonged circulation delay (as in congestive heart failure) produces the crescendo-decrescendo Cheyne-Stokes pattern (p.2282).

Treatment of CSA has NOT been shown to improve long-term health outcomes, so specific treatment is generally indicated only for symptomatic CSA; unlike OSA, treatment is difficult and depends on the underlying cause (p.2282).
harrison.pathophysiology: In OSA the pharyngeal airway lacks fixed bony/cartilaginous support, so patency depends on pharyngeal dilator muscles. Inspiration generates increasingly negative intraluminal pressure (a suctioning force); at sleep onset neuromuscular output to these muscles declines, and in a collapsible airway this causes transient pharyngeal collapse (apnoea) or near-collapse (hypopnoea), typically terminated by an arousal that restores muscle activity. Collapse sites include the soft palate (most common), tongue base, lateral pharyngeal walls, and epiglottis. OSA is often worst in REM sleep (lowest skeletal-muscle output) and supine (gravity). A small pharyngeal lumen (soft-tissue enlargement from fat, lymphoid tissue, or genetic variation; craniofacial factors such as mandibular retroposition/micrognathia), low lung volume (reduced caudal pharyngeal traction, pronounced in obesity), and high nasal resistance all predispose to collapse. Pharyngeal muscle activation is linked to ventilatory drive: an over-sensitive ventilatory control system, a low arousal threshold (preempting CO2-mediated muscle compensation), or a high arousal threshold (prolonging apnoeas) all contribute. In OSA-related disease, sleep fragmentation, cortical arousals, and intermittent hypoxaemia/hypercapnia drive sympathetic overactivity, blood-pressure surges, a prothrombotic/proinflammatory state, insulin resistance, and large negative intrathoracic pressure swings that alter cardiac preload/afterload and promote cardiac/electrical remodelling. CSA is usually caused by increased PCO2 sensitivity producing hyperventilation alternating with apnoea, plus prolonged circulatory delay (heart failure) giving Cheyne-Stokes breathing.
additionalDifferentials: Narcolepsy (multiple sleep latency / maintenance of wakefulness testing helps distinguish from OSA)
Insomnia (common in the general population, may coexist with OSA)
nonInfectiousMimics: Cheyne-Stokes / central sleep apnoea of heart failure
additionalInvestigations: Home sleep test (respiratory and cardiac channels) for cost-effective diagnosis
Apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI) and respiratory disturbance index (RDI) quantification
Overnight oximetry profile (mean, nadir, time at low saturation)
Multiple sleep latency test / maintenance of wakefulness test (quantify sleepiness, distinguish narcolepsy)
Upper-airway imaging (cephalometry, MRI, CT) and fibreoptic endoscopy to identify anatomic risk factors (not routine; useful for surgical planning)
Cardiac evaluation for systolic/diastolic dysfunction or structural abnormality
Overnight blood-pressure monitoring (may show nondipping pattern)
Arterial blood gas (usually normal awake; waking hypoxaemia/hypercarbia suggests cardiopulmonary disease or hypoventilation)
Drug-induced sleep endoscopy (for hypoglossal-nerve stimulation candidacy)
redFlags: Waking hypoxaemia or hypercarbia, suggesting coexisting cardiopulmonary disease or a hypoventilation syndrome
Evidence of cor pulmonale, suggesting a comorbid cardiopulmonary condition (OSA alone is NOT thought to cause right-heart failure)
Excessive daytime sleepiness with occupational accident or motor-vehicle-crash risk (drowsy driving)
Coexisting heart failure (raises risk of both OSA and CSA)
Severe nocturnal hypoxaemia with elevated haemoglobin
harrison.prognosis: OSA is the most common medical cause of daytime sleepiness and reduces quality of life. It is strongly associated with cardiac, cerebrovascular and metabolic disease (coronary artery disease, heart failure with and without reduced EF, atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, atherosclerosis, stroke, diabetes), premature death, and increased risk of certain cancers. Untreated OSA carries a roughly twofold risk of occupational accidents and a two- to threefold increase in motor-vehicle crashes. CPAP improves alertness, mood, quality of life, blood pressure and insulin sensitivity, but randomized trials have NOT shown that CPAP reduces cardiovascular/stroke events or prolongs survival. CSA carries increased risk for heart failure and atrial fibrillation, and its treatment has not been shown to improve long-term outcomes; adaptive servoventilation showed no cardiovascular or mortality benefit and increased mortality in patients with LVEF below 45%.
pitfalls: Assuming absence of snoring excludes OSA - pharyngeal collapse can occur without tissue vibration.
Assuming a normal weight excludes OSA - absence of obesity does NOT exclude the diagnosis.
Underrecognising OSA in women, who have a lower arousal threshold, shorter and more REM-predominant apnoeas, and tend to report fatigue/insomnia rather than classic sleepiness.
Relying on symptoms/signs to gauge severity - they do not accurately predict the severity of sleep-related breathing disturbance; objective measurement is required.
Treating a single negative home sleep study as definitive when prior probability is high - follow with PSG.
Attributing right-heart failure/cor pulmonale to OSA alone, which is not thought to cause it - look for a comorbid cardiopulmonary condition.
Using adaptive servoventilation in patients with CSA and LVEF below 45% (FDA warning following increased mortality).
Sedative-hypnotics have inconsistent effects and should be avoided in most patients with moderate-to-severe OSA; opioids worsen CSA in a dose-dependent way.
harrison.severityClassification: OSA severity by apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI = apnoeas plus hypopnoeas per hour of sleep): mild OSAHS = AHI 5-14 events/h; moderate OSAHS = AHI 15-29 events/h; severe OSAHS = AHI at least 30 events/h. The respiratory disturbance index (RDI) additionally counts respiratory effort-related arousals (RERAs). Each AHI level can be further qualified by the degree of sleepiness and associated hypoxaemia (Table 308-2, p.2280).
